title: H.264
subtitle: H.264 framing from a headless Linux desktop to the Windows media bridge, so an AI meeting attendee can share a terminal or browser as it works.
lede: Helix puts a digital employee in Teams meetings, and people wanted to watch it work: a browser page it was reading, a terminal it was typing into. I decided the employee would share a real screen through Teams' own screen-sharing path, with H.264 as the video format end to end. A headless Linux desktop (virtual display, window manager, Chromium, terminal) is captured and encoded by FFmpeg as an H.264 elementary stream. The employee can share a browser, a terminal or the whole desktop, and stop cleanly. Terminal text is typed at a pace people can follow, faster for long outputs so large updates finish.
quote: I picked a low frame rate on purpose, because the content is text and the bandwidth is better spent on sharpness.
evidence: Microsoft Teams real-time media: an AI participant sharing a browser, terminal or desktop into Teams as H.264 over the existing authenticated meeting connection.
Binary wire protocol design: a small frame contract carrying one H.264 access unit per frame between a Rust voice engine and a C# media bridge, cut on access-unit boundaries.
Video encoding for legibility: a low frame rate and stream headers repeated at every keyframe, so a late joiner or reconnected bridge starts decoding within a couple of seconds.
author: Corey James
